name: Power efficiency
answer: These measures show how much of the power a data center draws reaches the computing equipment, and how hard each rack is pushed. Dense GPU racks draw far more power than older server halls, so efficiency and density decide how much AI compute a site can run on the power it has.

metrics.line: The ratio of everything a facility draws from the grid to what its IT equipment alone consumes. A PUE of 1.5 means half again as much power goes to cooling, power conversion, and lighting as goes to the servers.
metrics.label: PUE, Power Usage Effectiveness

metrics.line: The same measurement as PUE expressed the other way round, IT energy as a percentage of total facility energy.
metrics.label: DCiE, Data Center Infrastructure Efficiency

metrics.line: Per-circuit measurement of how much of each breaker's rated capacity is in use, tracked continuously and at peak.
metrics.label: Breaker-level load and peak draw

metrics.line: The kilowatts delivered to and dissipated by a single rack. Traditional enterprise racks ran 5 to 15 kW; dense GPU training racks are specified at 40 to over 100 kW.
metrics.label: Power density per rack

reading.body:
Power efficiency in a data center is measured by how much of the grid draw reaches the IT equipment and how hard each rack is pushed, and dense GPU racks now demand 40 to over 100 kW where traditional enterprise racks ran 5 to 15 kW.

PUE and DCiE are the same fact stated two ways. PUE is total facility power divided by IT power, so a PUE of 1.5 means half again as much power goes to cooling, conversion, and lighting as goes to the servers. DCiE expresses IT energy as a percentage of total facility energy. Both describe overhead, not useful compute, and both are ratios, so a facility can improve its PUE while consuming more power in absolute terms.

Power density per rack is the number that ties efficiency to AI capacity. A rack specified at 40 to over 100 kW draws several times what an enterprise rack drew, so the same building and the same grid connection support far fewer racks when those racks are GPU training hardware. Breaker-level load and peak draw make the constraint concrete: each circuit has a rated capacity, and the site can only run as many racks as its circuits and its supply can carry at peak.

What this data does not give is any actual measured value for a specific facility. It defines the metrics and states the rack-density range, but no PUE figure, no DCiE figure, and no site-level load data appear here. It also does not cover where the power comes from, how it is cooled, or what it costs, which are separate subjects.
